message.content: {"summary":"Outstanding work. Your report met every task requirement: you identified several ethical issues and linked them to engineering design, built balanced for/against arguments, and supported everything with eight credible references and four external case studies. Your decision rule in Figure 1 and multi-stakeholder recommendations were practical and well justified. Presentation was fluent, with tables and a flowchart used competently. This is an excellent, publication-quality piece of ethical analysis.","next_steps":["Tighten your abstract to the ~150-word target; it currently runs slightly over, and concise abstracts are a professional skill worth practising.","When using analogies like WannaCry, strengthen the bridge by discussing how ransomware outage data might (or might not) transfer to hardware defect risk, beyond acknowledging the limitation.","Push toward deeper quantitative analysis of your own scenario: e.g., estimate or bound the defect-escape cost for Rachel's servers to complement the external case-study figures."],"criteria":{"C1":"Excellent. You identified several ethical issues — test coverage set by the release calendar, the data-loss rule, and conflict of interest — and linked each to engineering design. Table 1 in your Introduction thoroughly mapped stakeholders, their stakes, and their decision power, demonstrating both organisational context and stakeholder understanding. To sustain this level in future work, keep pairing every issue with an explicit stakeholder impact statement as you did here.","C2":"Excellent. Your for/against arguments were objective and appropriately deep, with each 'for' argument (e.g., competitive advantage from on-time shipping) critically weakened for this specific contract. Your recommendations gave distinct decision-making guidance for five stakeholder groups, including her company, the health department, and the chip supplier. Next level is already achieved; maintain this discipline of testing every argument against the specific contract context.","C3":"Excellent. Your structure — arguments for, against, decision rule, options, and the most ethical path — built logically to a conclusion that restated the argument chain, e.g., 'ship only when the risk has been measured, reduced where practical and accepted by an informed customer.' Figure 1 and the tables reinforced the systematic treatment of all stakeholders. This is compelling, well-scaffolded argumentation; keep using visual anchors to carry the logical thread.","C4":"Excellent. Eight credible references (NAO, Leveson & Turner, HBR, DOJ, standards) combined quantitative evidence — 81 of 236 trusts disrupted, 19,000 cancelled appointments, $475M and $4.3B figures — with qualitative evidence from four external case studies, balanced across both sides of the argument. To go further, consider adding scenario-specific quantitative estimates so evidence speaks directly to Rachel's case, not only to analogous incidents.","C5":"Excellent. Your writing was fluent, concise, and error-free, with all required sections present and functioning. Two tables and the Figure 1 decision flowchart were used competently to support the discussion, and your IEEE-style references were consistent and relevant. The only refinement is the slightly over-length abstract. Sustain this standard; consider adding one more visual type (e.g., a stakeholder influence map) in future reports."}}
message.reasoning: Produce JSON feedback. All excellent marks. Summary ≤80 words, next_steps 3 items, criteria ≤70 words each.
